parts: Name this quantum effect in which an electromagnetic potential affects the interference between possible paths for a charge carrier. In one form of this effect, the wave function of a particle shifts passing around a solenoid, even with a negligible magnetic field.
At the nanoscale, sawtooth-shaped voltage oscillations can occur due to this quantum phenomenon, in which electrons can move across a classically impenetrable potential barrier.

Two tunneling junctions and a gate capacitor connect three electrodes to an island in the ‘single electron’ variety of these devices. Altering the gate voltage applied to a metal oxide layer allows current flow in another type of these devices.

bonuses.leadin: Meir of Rothenburg introduced an addition to this declaration that allows for sinners and “transgressors of the Law” to pray with the congregation. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this Aramaic declaration whose English translation ends with “our vows are no longer vows, and our prohibitions are no longer prohibitions, and our oaths are no longer oaths”. In the 12th century, Rabbi Meir ben Samuel altered this declaration to change the tense from the past to the future.
Kol Nidre is recited before sunset to begin this Jewish Day of Atonement, usually held in late September or early October.

Kol Nidre appears in this prayer book, used on Yom Kippur and Rosh Hashanah. This book, which has a name that translates to “cycle”, is distinct from the Siddur, which is typically used for weekday and Shabbat services.

bonuses.leadin: In this video game, owls and ducks have a very low chance to make human noises. For 10 points each:
parts: Identify this action-adventure game developed by Re-Logic. Often nicknamed “2D Minecraft”, this sandbox game contains bosses such as the Moon Lord and Plantera.

In Terraria, this boss is likely the first one the player will encounter as it spawns automatically at a relatively early level of the game. This boss has a similarly named “brain” counterpart that spawns in the Crimson biome.

After defeating the Eye of Cthulhu, the player will often create one of these structures which can give them access to the lowest level of the Terraria world. These structures allow the player character to “fall” to a lava-filled biome.

bonuses.leadin: In this work, a boy is described as “charging madly into space” while his sisters play with dolls. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this short story in which the whispering of “there must be more money” drives Paul to use the title object to “get there”, eventually dying after shouting “Malabar! It’s Malabar!” and declaring “I am lucky!”
This author wrote short stories such as “The Rocking-Horse Winner” and also courted controversy with the sexually explicit passages of his novels Women in Love and Lady Chatterley’s Lover.

Lawrence’s time staying in Taos was recounted in a memoir by Mabel Dodge Luhan, which directly inspired this author’s 2021 novel Second Place. A novel consisting of the conversations of an unnamed novelist who travels to Athens is the first in this author’s Outline trilogy.

bonuses.leadin: A wiry figure with two faces and pink hands appears in the lower right of this painting. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this painting that depicts a scene of “aquatic, celestial and earthly entities.” Also including a clock trapped in a golden cage, this painting uses similar techniques to its artist’s other work Twittering Machine.

The painter of Fish Magic, Paul Klee (“CLAY”), was heavily influenced by this art movement, pioneered by Salvador Dalí and Joan Miró among others. This movement’s namesake manifesto was written by André Breton.

Fish Magic and The Twittering Machine both prominently use this technique to create a murky background. This technique, similar to watercolour, creates an opaque surface by utilising a binding agent, usually gum.

bonuses.leadin: This event was caused by the election of Pope Urban VI and the accusations of intimidation which led to his election. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this event, during which there were two or three claimants to the Papacy, residing in Rome, France and, for a brief period, Pisa. This event is sometimes described as “great”, causing confusion with a separate event of 1054.
During the Western Schism, the French-supported claimants lived in this city. This French city had been the site of the papal residence since Clement V moved it there in 1309.
The Western Schism ended with the election of Pope Martin V after this council, the first to be convened in the Holy Roman Empire. This council also condemned Jan Hus (“YAN HOOS”) as a heretic.

bonuses.leadin: This protein transfers electrons between the third and fourth complex in the electron transport chain. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this protein whose presence outside the mitochondria activates caspases, causing apoptosis (“app-op-TOE-sis”).
Inside the mitochondria, cytochrome C is primarily bound to these lipids. Oxidation of these lipids in damaged cells causes a release of cytochrome C.
Cytochrome C is a heme-protein, meaning it possesses a ring containing this metal. This metal is also present in haemoglobin in red blood cells.

bonuses.leadin: Note to players: description acceptable. Dennis Lindley used this belief to justify the need for Cromwell’s rule, arguing it was a counterpoint to the idea that something having zero probability means its likelihood cannot be influenced by data. For 10 points each:
parts: Describe this belief, first recorded in a collection by John Hayward, that likely originates as a 16th century metaphor for fraud. This belief is central to an apocryphal story about West Country smugglers, which itself inspired a nickname for Swindon Town FC fans.

Even earlier, a medieval Rabbinic fable features one of these creatures tricking a wolf into gnawing at the moon’s reflection in the belief it is made of cheese. Another one of these creatures fought and defeated the wolf Isengrim.

A more recent example of the moon being made of cheese is in this 1989 short film, the first to feature Wallace and Gromit, in which they travel to the moon in search of Wensleydale after running out on a bank holiday.

bonuses.leadin: Accompanied by Theodore Roosevelt, this man organised a 1914 expedition to explore the River of Doubt. For 10 points each:
parts: Identify this military officer and explorer who established a commission to improve communications throughout Mato Grosso state to aid indigenous people. A state with its capital at Porto Velho (“POR-too VAY-oo”) is named after this man.
Rondon was a supporter of the rights of indigenous people in this home country of his. Rondon served in the military during the 1924 São Paulorevolt in this country.

Rondon’s involvement in the 1930 Brazilian Revolution helped overthrow a system of politics often known by this phrase. This phrase refers to a popular beverage and characterises a system dominated by landed gentry and oligarchy.

bonuses.leadin: This novel was published under the pseudonym “The Scoffing Scholar of Lanling”, the identity of its author having remained unknown to this day. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this novel, which follows the experiences of the corrupt merchant Ximen Qing (“SHEE-men CHING”) and his many sexual partners. The erotic content in this novel caused it to be heavily suppressed by authorities.

Many characters in Jin Ping Mei originate from the earlier novel Water Margin, such as this character, who confronts Ximen Qing at Lion Tower. In Water Margin, this character is nicknamed “Pilgrim” and kills Pan Jinlian.

Another Ming dynasty work is this other classic Chinese novel, that follows a monk on a pilgrimage to a mythical version of India. This novel also includes the story of Sun Wukong, who is trapped under a mountain for five centuries.

bonuses.leadin: In the detective novel Clouds of Witness, a farmer sings this tune while rescuing Lord Peter Wimsey from a bog. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this song sung to the hymn tune "Cranbrook" that tells of ducks eating worms that were, in turn, eating the body of a person who had died due to cold.

"Cranbrook", the tune to which "On Ilkla Moor Baht 'at" is sung, is also the tune of a song titled "While [these people] watched their flocks". A different Christian hymn based on Psalm 23 is titled "The Lord is my [one of these people]".

“On Ilkla Moor Baht ‘at” is recorded as numbers 2143 and 19808 in this index of English-language folk songs, begun by its namesake in 1970, which comprises nearly 25,000 works and is now readily available online.

bonuses.leadin: Planes containing points in these structures can be defined by Miller indices. For 10 points each:
parts: Name these regular arrangements of atoms or ions, made up of multiple unit cells.
Along with hexagonal close packed, this Bravais (“bra-VAY”) lattice arrangement has the highest possible packing fraction. There are four atoms per unit cell in this lattice arrangement.
This other lattice structure is made up of two overlapping face centered cubic lattices for different elements. This structure is common in semiconductors such as gallium arsenide.

bonuses.leadin: This figure and her son are freed from captivity after being exchanged for a pregnant mouse, which is actually their captor’s wife. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this magical woman who was framed for the murder of her son when he was taken by a monster while her maids slept.
Rhiannon and her son Pryderi, King of Dyfed (“DUV-ved”), are key figures in the Mabinogi, which are myths from this constituent country of the United Kingdom.

Another monster from Welsh mythology is this water dwelling creature, whose depictions range between looking like a crocodile and a furry mammal. According to one myth, this monster is hunted everyday by three men who are killed and brought back to life each time.

bonuses.leadin: This work was publicly condemned in the Synod of Dordrecht for arguing that prophecies have only natural explanations. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this philosophical work that claims that the Torah was not written by Moses and that it was essentially a political constitution for ancient Israel. Critiquing organised religion, this work argues that God does not act for a particular end goal.
The Tractatus Theologico-Politicus was written by this 17th century Dutch philosopher, who interrupted writing his Ethics to respond to religious intolerance in his home country.

Spinoza’s ideas inspired this Jewish thinker, who became embroiled in the ‘pantheism controversy’ with Freidrich Heinrich Jacobi. This thinker published his views on Judaism in a secularising society, and his criticisms of Prussian monarchism, in his 1783 work Jerusalem.

bonuses.leadin: In the preface to a translation of poems from this country, an author described the excitement of being “suddenly introduced to a new and magnificent literature.” For 10 points each:
parts: Name this country whose poetry was translated by Ezra Pound into a collection which includes “The River Merchant’s Wife.” Other works of poetry from this modern-day country include “Quiet Night Thought”.

With Florence Ayscough (“ASS-kew”), a poet with this surname made free adaptations of Li Bai in her collection Fir-Flower Tablets. A description of a “drowned sailor” found “off Madaket” begins a poem by an author with this surname that ends “The Lord survives the rainbow of His will.”

Amy Lowell calls her lover “white and shining” as she does this activity in a poem that describes “the scent of the lilacs” “heavy with stillness.” A section of “Song of Myself” describes “twenty-eight young men” doing this activity who are joined by a woman who “saw them and loved them.”

bonuses.leadin: This person became the youngest person to be appointed Chief Nursing Officer for England in 1999. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this former Bishop of London who was installed as the first female Archbishop of Canterbury on 25 March 2026.

To get from London to Canterbury for her installation, Mullally followed this pilgrimage path from St. Paul’s Cathedral to Canterbury Cathedral. This pilgrimage path is named for the Archbishop of Canterbury installed in 1162.

This anthem by Joanna Marsh was sung during the installation. This anthem sets lines from Julian of Norwich’s Revelations of Divine Love to music and is titled for a famous hopeful phrase used by Julian.

bonuses.leadin: The Agnus Dei of a mass named for this song uses a double canon in the upper voices and a retrograde cantus firmus in the bass. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this secular song used as a cantus firmus in many masses of the 15th and 16th centuries. Both Jesus and Charles the Bold have been proposed as the title figure of this song.

Among the composers to write L’homme armé masses is Cristóbal de Morales, whose other major cantus firmus mass is based on this chanson (“SHON-SON”) attributed to Josquin des Prez (“dess prez”). The speaker of this chanson feels “such painful distress” at leaving his lover.
This later Italian composer wrote two “L’homme armé” masses, but is better known for his Pope Marcellus Mass, which is apocryphally said to have “saved polyphony” from the Catholic Church.

bonuses.leadin: This scheme would create a new tripoint border in the village of Six Ashes in Shropshire. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this scheme agreed in 1405 in which Edmund Mortimer and two other nobles would split the kingdom of England and the territories of King Henry IV.

Edmund Mortimer joined the scheme after his capture by this Welsh leader, who was rebelling against Henry IV at the time. This leader called the first Welsh parliament at Machynlleth (“muh-KUNTH-leth”) and is the only native-born holder of the title of “Prince of Wales” since Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (“GRIFF-ith”)

As part of the Tripartite Indenture, Henry Percy was to become king of this kingdom, named for the earldom he already held. Stretching from Scotland to Warwickshire and Norfolk, this kingdom shares a name with a modern-day county in Northern England.

bonuses.leadin: One artifact from this civilisation was a jade mosaic mask of a “bat god”. For 10 points each:
parts: Identify this pre-Columbian civilisation which had its capital at Monte Albán. The first known artifact that includes this civilisation’s writing is a danzante (“dahn-SAHN-tay”) stone depicting a dead and bloodied man strung upside-down.

This Zapotec site is the second-most important behind Monte Albán for archaeologists as a religious centre. Later being overtaken by the Mixtecs, this site is the only example in the region of detailed and overly decorative stone mosaics.
The Zapotecs flourished in what is now Oaxaca (“wa-HA-ka”) state in this modern-day country, also home to the Olmec and Maya civilisations.

bonuses.leadin: In the 5th century, Latin replaced Ogham as the main script used to write one language in this family. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this language family that includes Manx, Scots Gaelic (“GAL-ick”) and Breton. Aidan Doyle has written a history of a language from this family “From the Norman Invasion to Independence”.

Many Celtic languages, such as Irish, use sentences that have this dominant word order, the third-most common globally. Other languages with this dominant word order include Arabic and Biblical Hebrew.

Irish makes much use of these context-bound reference words, which include the verbs tar, meaning “come”, and téigh (“TAYG”), meaning “go”. Charles J. Fillmore outlined three main types of these words: personal, spatial, and temporal.

bonuses.leadin: This mathematician gives his name to a process which is an example of a continuous time Markov chain. For 10 points each:
parts: Which French mathematician names a discrete distribution whose mean is equal to its variance?

The Poisson distribution is part of this family of distributions, specifically when the power parameter p is equal to one. The normal and inverse Gaussian distributions are part of this family, whose distributions are a special case of exponential dispersion models.

When p equals two, the Tweedie distribution is equal to this two-parameter distribution, whose special cases include the chi-squared distribution. The denominator of this distribution’s PDF contains a function equal to the integral from zero to infinity of [read slowly] t to the alpha minus one, times e to the minus t with respect to t.

bonuses.leadin: One novel by this author is narrated by the fungi living in the floorboards of its setting, an all-male sanatorium in the Sudeten Mountains. For 10 points each:
parts: Name this author of The Empusium. In another novel by this author, the protagonist and her neighbour find a man dead from seemingly choking on a deer bone, though she believes that he was actually murdered.
Tokarczuk was awarded the 2018 edition of this award. This major literary award was won in 2025 by Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai (“LAZ-loh KRAZ-na-HOR-kye”).

Besides Tokarczuk, the Nobel Prize has also been awarded to four other Poles, including this writer and poet who discussed his experiences of Stalinism in The Captive Mind. This writer states that “no one believes it is happening now” in his poem, “A Song on the End of the World”.
